CMR (Chen et al., 2023) conditions a Taobao re-ranker on a preference vector through a hypernetwork and trains it with REINFORCE on the preference-weighted list reward, so that operators can move along the trade-off at serving time without retraining; its online experiments show each metric responding roughly monotonically to its own preference weight (Figure 5). TSCAC (Cai et al., 2023) treats watch time as the primary return and interactions as constraints in a constrained MDP, trains auxiliary actor–critics first and then the main policy under a proximity constraint; fully launched at Kuaishou, it gained 0.379% watch time and 3.376% shares while comments fell 0.619%. Two lessons carry across all three layers. The weights that balance training losses, the weights that fuse predicted scores at serving time, and the business preference over outcomes are different objects — PAPERec is interesting precisely because it ties the first to the third — and an MOO method must be evaluated at the layer it actually changes. And a Pareto-stationary training objective does not imply a Pareto-optimal online operating point: every paper above reports at least one secondary metric that moved the wrong way.

sourceOccurrences.context: Search ranking shares the multi-objective structure of recommendation — a primary relevance or purchase objective plus secondary objectives such as revenue, product quality, defect rate, delivery speed, brand mix, and, in autocomplete, the quality of the suggested query — but differs in three respects that change how gradient-based MOO is applied. The dominant production rankers are still gradient-boosted trees in the LambdaMART family, so gradients are taken with respect to the *scores* $\mathbf{s}$ rather than model parameters and each boosting round fits a tree to a combined pseudo-gradient $g(\mathbf{s}) = \sum_k \alpha_k \nabla_{\mathbf{s}} C_k(\mathbf{s})$; the target metrics (NDCG, purchase NDCG) are non-differentiable and are optimized through metric-weighted pairwise surrogates; and the requirements arrive from stakeholders as bounds — "improve relevance as much as possible while keeping revenue within −1% of production" — which makes a constrained formulation more natural than a scalarization. Early work at Microsoft already reflected this: Svore et al. (2011) modified the lambda gradients so that a click-derived objective could improve only where it did not hurt human-judged relevance, a lexicographic rather than weighted combination.

sourceOccurrences.context: **Preference-directed and robust combinations.** When the number of objectives grows, bounds become hard to set and the preference-directed methods of the MOO literature become relevant. Mahapatra et al. (2023) bring EPO, weighted-Chebyshev MGDA, augmented-Lagrangian and dynamic-barrier combinations into the boosting loop by computing all of them on score-space gradients and fitting trees to the result, and evaluate on Amazon labels for purchase, historical purchase, relevance, brandedness and delivery speed. Their main practical finding is that the per-iteration combination coefficients fluctuate badly in a tree ensemble and must be smoothed with a moving average before the preference is actually tracked — the boosting analogue of MultiBalance's EMA. The evaluation is offline; the companion MO-LightGBM library (Dong & Momma, 2025) makes the twelve variants reproducible. A different route is taken by Singh et al. (2023) for query autocomplete, where a neural pairwise ranker must balance customer-behavior ranking against query quality. Rather than fix the mixture, they train with ALMO (Cortes et al., 2020), a min–max formulation that optimizes against the worst admissible mixture of the two losses while the mixture weights are learned jointly. A four-week A/B test on one million prefixes raised GMV by 0.26% and shopping-item diversity by 0.41%; the public AOL experiment in the same paper shows an MRR decline, so the robustness is against the mixture, not a guarantee that every metric improves.
